overview: After 1.Nc3 c5 2.Rb1 White prepares b4 to hit the Sicilian-style c5 pawn with an early queenside expansion. The rook move loses time and the b-pawn is not yet ready, so Black simply develops with ...Nc6 or ...e5 and ...d5. It is a rare surprise move with little theory.

white_ideas.idea: Play b4 to challenge c5 and gain space
Develop the king's knight and a g3 fianchetto behind the b-pawn

black_ideas.idea: Treat it as a reversed Sicilian and develop normally

typical_structures.structure: Closed Sicilian-style structures with an early b4

character.notes: Not forcing and not especially safe for White, and it neither wins nor loses by force.

soundness.notes: Playable but loses time, so Black may get easy equality.

approach.notes: Strong players seldom start with 1.Nc3 and 2.Rb1.

level.notes: Neither much to remember nor hard to play.
